question: How can I upskill managers across my company without building courses in-house?
text:
Yes. You can build a strong manager-development system without becoming a course-production company. The trick is to outsource the content and facilitation, while keeping ownership of the manager standards, practice, and accountability internally.

A practical model

I’d use a “buy + curate + practice” model:

Define your manager expectations internally

What does a good manager at your company actually do?

E.g. run effective 1:1s, give feedback, delegate, manage performance, hire well, handle conflict, develop people.

Keep this to ~6–10 core capabilities.

Buy the learning content
Rather than creating videos and courses, license an existing library or use an external provider.

Options range from broad learning libraries to specialist manager-development platforms. In the DACH market, for example, Haufe Akademie offers thousands of courses plus live, blended and in-house formats; Masterplan offers a large multilingual digital library. 
K
Kurslotse
+1

Use cohorts for the important stuff
Don't rely on "watch these 12 videos." For critical management behaviors, put managers into 6–12 week cohorts with live facilitators, peer discussion and assignments.

Platforms such as Growthspace, for example, offer small expert-led cohorts focused on specific skills rather than generic leadership curricula. 
G
Growthspace

Add coaching where it matters
Give senior or struggling managers access to 1:1 coaching rather than trying to give everyone the same experience. Current enterprise offerings include BetterUp, CoachHub, Torch, Growthspace and others, with different mixes of coaching, cohorts and mentoring. 
B
Boon

Make the manager's actual job the classroom

Every module should end with something like:

"Have the performance conversation you've been avoiding this week."

Then have the manager reflect with their cohort, coach or manager.

Measure behavior, not course completion

Instead of reporting "92% completed Manager Fundamentals," measure things such as:

Quality of 1:1s

Employee feedback on manager effectiveness

Performance-management quality

Internal mobility/development conversations

Manager confidence before/after

Retention or engagement trends

What I'd outsource vs. keep internal
Keep internal	Buy externally
Your manager competency model	Course content
Your leadership principles	Facilitators
Company-specific policies	Coaching
Business scenarios/context	Assessments
Expectations of managers	Learning platform
Manager accountability	Specialist expertise

This distinction is important. You don't need to own the content; you need to own the definition of "good management" at your company.

Three good approaches
1. Lowest effort: learning library

Give managers access to a strong external catalogue and curate a handful of recommended learning paths.

Good if you have hundreds/thousands of managers and relatively limited L&D capacity.

For example, PPG describes using an internal hub that connects employees to external resources such as LinkedIn Learning rather than producing everything internally.

2. Best balance: external manager academy

Buy an existing manager curriculum and run it as a company-wide cohort program.

For example:

12 weeks

Week 1 — Role of the manager

Week 2 — Setting expectations

Week 3 — 1:1s

Week 4 — Feedback

Week 5 — Delegation

Week 6 — Coaching

Week 7 — Motivation

Week 8 — Conflict

Week 9 — Performance management

Week 10 — Difficult conversations

Week 11 — Developing people

Week 12 — Leading through change

The provider supplies the content and facilitator. Your L&D team supplies the context and keeps managers accountable.

This would be my default recommendation for most companies.

3. Scalable/modern: content + AI practice + coaching

For a very large manager population, combine an external content library with an AI practice/coaching layer and reserve human coaching for higher-need managers.

There are now platforms specifically designed to put manager practice into tools such as Slack or Teams rather than requiring managers to visit another LMS. 
B
blify.co

One thing I'd avoid

Don't buy a giant leadership catalogue and call it a manager-development strategy.

You can end up with 10,000 courses and no consistent answer to:

"What should every manager in our company be able to do?"

Instead, create a one-page manager capability framework, then map external content onto it.

That gives you the economics of outsourcing without outsourcing your management philosophy.

If you tell me roughly how many managers you have, their locations/languages, and your approximate budget per manager/year, I can shortlist 5–7 external providers and show you what I'd buy for a company your size.
